segments.description: All right, coaches, welcome to our afternoon session. It gives me great pleasure to introduce Marion Patoli. Marion is a player who won an impressive 8WTA titles and reached a career high of number eight in the world, along with the famous 2013 Wimbledon title. A fierce competitor on the court, Marion has now transitioned to a new career, currently helping out a couple of athletes, one of those being Yelena, Austin Panko, and also doing some commentary for the Grand Slam. We are honoured to have you here today, Marion, for this live Q&A session. And coaches, if you do have any questions for Marion, please put them in the Q&A function of the court. Marion, a warm welcome from Australia. How are we? Thank you so much. I'm good, guys. I'm so happy to be with you today and share my experience. It has been a long journey to start from very small village in France, all the way to lifting that trophy on the Wimbledon Center Court. But if I can share my journey and help you as coaches to answer your questions, your doubts or whatever you might have in terms of uncertainty, which is definitely part of the job and the journey. I would be more than happy to do so. Perfect. Well, we will get straight into it because we've had a couple of questions already, Marion. And one of those is a fairly tricky question to answer to start off with. But in Australia, we have a fairly high drop off rate in girls' tennis, particularly around

that sort of 12 to 14 age group. Do you have any tips for our coaches to help maintain the girls in our sport? Yeah. Well, it's actually really the age for girls when you're deciding what you want to do. And usually before you pick up tennis, but not only tennis, you're doing multi-sports. That was my case when I was younger. I was doing tennis and classical ballet. So even though I was coming from a very small village, it was still available for me to do two or three sports activity outside of school. And as you grow, then you realize that if you start to move into, in terms of the rankings and your progression, you have to decide which one to pick. And usually tennis is not the one the girls are picking because it's very individual sports. And they feel very much alone and lonely on the court. And this is a feeling especially for a girl in the psychological part of a girl that is sometimes a little too hard to deal with. And therefore they prefer to go into team sports or sport they're doing with all the friends so they don't feel that alone. So my biggest advice and the one that I felt for me that kept me in the sport is even though it's an individual sport, try to always bring girls together to play together at that moment because you're going to still emulate them towards trying to improve their level, towards trying to win that local tournament which is happening at the weekend or just reaching

that next wall. But by keeping them together, you don't exaggerate that feeling of loneliness, which is really something that could be difficult for girls. So for example, it's very interesting, I'm coaching here in Dubai, two young athletes, one girl is 12 and one boy is 12. And the boy got COVID, so he has been isolated since 10 days. So I'm only coaching the girl and for her to be only alone on the court with me, she's finding that more difficult that when she's playing against that boy and with that boy. So even though sometimes the practice are hard and they're fighting because one wants to win, the other one doesn't want to lose, you still create that emulation and they feel a lot happier. So really my main answer to that is trying to keep that sort of together feeling almost like team bounding really. When you create those relationships between kids, you create friendship and that way through, they don't feel it's really only themself on the court having to fight to beat someone on the other side of the net. Great answer. And when you grew up in France, was there a big team-based competition over there or was it mainly an individual sport still? It was mainly individual but the beauty of France and the way France work and that was really for me a huge advantage looking back at it now. You can play as a young 10, 11, 12 years old, you have only an adult ranking. So because you have already an adult ranking, you can participate in all what we call open

tournaments which is basically for any age and it goes from non-ranking towards whatever is the best ranking available in that region basically. And therefore when you're 11 or 12, you're still going to play against a lot of players who are higher ranked in front of you. So you're going to have all those matches under your belt and when I was already 11 or 12, I was playing about 100 matches a year against adults. And for me that training base to play against different style of players was very, very rich because I might play against someone almost my age for example who is trying also to become someone great. I might play against someone who is 45 or 50 years old who used to have an old style, we're playing only size, I might play against someone who comes to the net. So all playing all this different game style really gave me that richness. So when I grew up and I came on to the tour and I played against someone who was serving for me, it was nothing new. I've done that already against adults in my youth or when I was playing against someone who is doing more drop shot or more slice, I've been facing that before. And it's really I think crucial for the kids to evaluate themselves against adults because if they play only against all the kids, mainly they have the same game style. It's about knocking up the ball from the back of the court and trying to sometimes come to the net, but it's very much the same game style they are all replicating.

Sometimes one is doing it better than the other one, but they are always facing the same same ball, same sort of rallies, it just constantly the same type of matches. And as they grow and develop and play on the tour, when they're going to face different game style, that's when sometimes the shock is a little bit too much and it's hard for their game to actually adapt. So for me, the way the French Federation are organizing their tournament schedule year around is actually a lot more tournaments for the adults and a lot less for the child. So as a child, you have to mix in with other adults because otherwise you literally can't play. And for me, actually, that was a massive plus into my grow as a tennis players and as also being able to face difficulties and face different challenge. Perfect. Now, let's go back to your youth a little bit. You talked a little bit about then and then you also talked about it in the presentation and you had such a growth mindset as a player and even as a young child, listening to some of the stories about you taking sort of responsibility for your own development, understanding it as being a very long process and almost understanding you've got to accept to do things a little bit differently to the others, to be able to find solutions and I guess solve some of the limitations you had within your game. And to do that at such a young age is unbelievably impressive and incredible.

So this is a two-part question. First part of it is, what were some of the things that made you able to identify it is such a long journey at such a young age? And then number two, what kind of advice have you got for our coaches today to help instill that growth mindset in the players that they're lucky enough to work with? It's a very interesting question. So when I was younger and I was doing all those fitness tests, I'm not sure if it's happening in tennis Australia as well, but basically what the French Federation is doing is they take the best kids by age group and they put them under a certain battery of fitness test and they see who comes out the best or have staggering numbers. They can identify to be great tennis players but also amazing athletes. That's how actually Amelie Moresmo, which is a dear friend and obviously an amazing French champion, came out really out of the blocks because she was having four years ahead of her age performance and she was having already not only four years ahead of the girls but four years ahead also on the boys level. So for example, when we were doing the ball throw, which is a very, you know, simple in the size, you take a slightly heavier ball than a tennis ball and you have to throw it from the base line, you have to go over the net. She was having the one that was going all over the baseline on the other side. I was the one that was landing on my service line on my side.

So I was basically like almost 20 meters compared to her. So, you know, it's just as a young tennis player who still wants to make it to not only a professional tennis level but wants to win a Grand Slam and you see the difference, you're like, whoa, okay, if I don't work towards that and if I don't find a solution still to have a good serve, I'm going to be limited at some point because, you know, I'm facing someone who is so much better than me that I have to find a solution. And so that was the way we were constantly working with my father is let's face a problem. Let's not go around it, but let's go through it so we find a solution to try to get me as close as possible to steal good end results. And if my serve would never be, let's say, my biggest weapon, we can still make it good enough for me to compete against a top player and then I can use another asset that might be better to compensate the sort of not weak serve but in a way average serve. So that was constantly our mindset is let's not just drop it because I'm too far, but let's find solution to keep me working. So I remember when my father saw me doing this, so obviously my shoulder was very weak and I had zero explosivity on my shoulder. I had to do 100 push ups on my own every single morning before going to school. And when you're 11 or 12 to do 100 full push up with your full body weight, it takes a long time.

I mean, it's not usually when you see 11 or 12 years old girls, especially girls, they have to do push ups on their knees. I mean, they can't do it fully and certainly not hundreds. So I had to wake up almost an hour and a half in advance to have enough time to do all those hundred push ups while we're going to school. So I made that always function that way with me. It's about giving me the sort of solution or at least trying to help me towards my problem, but I had to take responsibility doing them alone. So it's also giving a responsibility to the child to see they're really motivated to make something great about their career or if you have to constantly tell them to do something. And that's where for me, you can really identify the ones who have that fire inside them, who really wants to succeed is when you're giving them something hard to do by themselves and they do it with the most amount of respect and the less amount of cheating. So if you usually put 10 kids to ask them to do every single day that exercise, you would see that a lot of them are going to drop. So either they will stop after 30 push ups or they will pretend they've done 100 that they want or some days they won't even do it at all. And you're going to see that that might be not the one that is the most talented, but you're going to see that one or two stubborn ones are going to stick to it and keep doing

it every single day. And that's what I saw also in Sam Stozer. So we are the same age. We start to play juniors together. And remember when I first saw her coming into Europe, she played that big group one in in Italy before Ron Gallo's junior. She was with a tennis Australian coach, I believe she was out of her home since like almost two months when you're only 15 or 16. It's not easy. She had to go play Ron Gallo's junior women's junior before she could go back to Australia. And she had to do all those bodies by herself. She was spending, I think two almost two to three hours every single day as a junior playing against the wall, just doing some bodies. And I remember looking at her, I was like, Jesus, I mean, that girl is going to be great. So back then I was better than her in terms of ranking on the juniors, but to see that amount of humility, going through everything she had to go through, because she was not the most talented one. But at the end, she won a grand slam as well, just like me. So it's all about those small details and those small mindsets that you can pick up into a kid that he might not be the beginning, the most talented one. But if he had that mindset, he might go a much longer way. The one I saluted, but slightly lazy. And talking about the small details and basically doing what you need to do to make, you know, have the best success possible and not cutting corners and things like that, you were very

famously known for your unique training regimes that you and your father did on court. I think I saw one clip of you at Wimbledon, I think it was before your semifinal. And you had ropes attached to your wrists that were attached to your waist that were attached to your knees and your ankles. And some of those are famously unique. Can you provide us a little bit of an insight into your father's thought process on how these specific training insights happened or occurred? So basically the way my father always functioned, and it was exactly the same way, actually, I was functioning as well, I was very slow. That was really my main problem. So I had an average, let's say, good stamina, but zero explosivity. So when I was playing, for example, against someone like Justin Enna or Kim Clashers or Amelie or Maria Sharapova or Serena or Venus, I could see very vividly the difference in term of fitness level, but not only the way that they can last on the court, I could last on the court as well, but just the difference of explosivity of power, general power that they were able to generate when they were waking up in the morning and just going into a regular warmup. And I couldn't do it with the best intention and the best willing to do it. My body was just not reacting. So we constantly had to find ways to stimulate my muscle and especially my fast muscle twist in order to give me that sort of explosivity level that I had to do and I had to have in

order to compete against those girls, because my goal was to beat them, which luckily enough I was able to beat all of them. But in order to arrive there, I had just had to train a lot more than them. But I was ready for that. It was not an issue for me that the most important thing at the end was to win, basically. And I was ready to do anything and whatever it takes just to win that match. But I knew to start with, we're just not starting with the same assets. It's just like if you have a car and your engine is 150 less horsepower than the one that you're trying to beat, you have to compensate with something. So if you don't build up your engine, if you don't work harder, then of course you're going to end up losing the race. So for me, that was, again, something I realized very early on when I was seeing them practicing, when I was playing in them in matches. I could see there were a second faster than me on the sprint dash, or I could see they were hitting the ball a lot harder or moving a lot better, but if I was doing all those explosivity exercises, and that's why for me working with elastic bands and against resistance was really my main core training because that was giving me the sort of explosivity to my muscle I needed. I knew if I was strong enough mentally to go through this in the morning of the match, I would have a shot to beat them. And that was the whole part of my career is basically something that was working at time

T was not working two months down the road because my muscle was getting used to it and we have to find another challenge, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. So it was constantly that sort of, you know, thinking process of saying, is this exercise going to last how long for how long we can keep it until it's going to drop in terms of intensity, we have to find something stronger, better, more difficult or whatever. And it was a constant thinking process actually was more difficult for me and my dad than just the stress of playing a tennis match because the stress of playing a tennis match. I always felt when I was ready, I could deal with it quite easily, but the worst feeling is going on court and you know, you're not ready. And that is just awful because you go on court, you want to try to chase that ball and your muscle are just not responding. And for me, that was constantly the most fear I had was just not to be ready for that challenge. So that's why I was constantly looking for a new training methods. I was doing my own research as well, see if I could pick something from another sport, especially track and field when they have to do a lot of explosivity work. And I can see now the evolution in tennis when you have so many more athletes, we're doing a lot more resistance training, we're doing a lot more sort of elastic bands type of training, a lot more going into the gym, a lot more having a private fitness coach

become because it's sort of a realization that it is essential and crucial into a whole development as a tennis player. And that was definitely a lot less when I used to play. So the girls were playing a lot more on the courts and we're training a lot more on the court, but we're spending a lot less time in the gym. So it was more natural athletes. And if you didn't have it, well, too bad for you. But for me, I realized early on that through fitness regime and through training, you can actually compensate your weakness. And yes, I was spending a lot of time on the tennis court, but also a lot of time in the gyms. And at the end, I got my reward. Well, you left no stone unturned, that's for sure. And speaking about your father, we caught up earlier on in preparation for this conference and I asked you a question around, have you always been a double handed player on both full hand and backhand? And you told me the story of how that eventuated. Did you want to share that with the coaches? Of course, of course. So I'm a natural lefty in life. I do everything with the left side. And funny enough, I can see my daughter already picking everything with the left side, which I'm happy about, but that's another story. And when I went on the court, so I was watching my dad and my brother playing for already two years. So I was going on the courts. I was just staying on the side playing with my toes and just looking at them playing every

day almost, because my dad was always very much a tennis enthusiastic and my brother as well. So I was almost going daily on the court, but just not playing. And one day I stood up on the court and said, well, now I want to play, but I played with the racket with my brother. And my brother is nine years older than me. So I started to take it up on the left side. But then my dad was like, no, no, taking on the right, because it's too difficult for me to show you the movement on the left side. I don't know how to do the full hand on the left side. So taking with the right side. And so the first time I played, I actually take the racket from the right side, but I do two handed backhand because I was using a lot my left hand on the two handed backhand. And apparently I don't remember it, obviously, but my dad told me that the first time he sent me some backhands to do, I put 50 balls over the net without missing. Just with a natural two handed backhand. And then my forehand was horrible because I have no, no strengths at all in the right side. So I was just going underspin forehand. He was going as a moon ball sort of an underspin move body was horrible. And then we saw in 1992, Monica Siles playing them wrong. I was fine all against Stephie Graf. And back then it was obviously in a national free TV. So we look at it and it was the first ever time we saw someone playing two handed on

both sides. We could, we didn't even knew it was like possible to play a two handed forehand because all the other players we would watch on TV would be, you know, Pete Sampras, Andrea Agassi, all those players playing just one handed regular forehands. So my dad was like, Oh, look at this. Maybe you should try the next day. I mean, she's doing two hands on both sides. You have a two good two handed backhand. You should maybe try and I try the next day. Obviously, I felt a lot better because I was using my left hand to help myself. And that's how I pick up the two handed on both sides. And then down the road, I eventually meet Monica. I even played against her in Miami and we become friends, which is unreal for me because she was my massive tennis idol growing up. I had posters of her all over my bedroom. I was playing in the same outfit as the one she was playing in tournaments. I was going to the shop buying the exact same dress. I was playing with the same racket as well. So to meet your idol one day and realize that actually, you know, they're proud of what you have been able to achieve. It's something quite incredible. You know, it's incredible to be able to and you can basically forget all the tests that the French Federation did with you in regards to the throwing test, because I'm sure if you had it in your left hand, you would have cleared the fences on the other side of the court.

That's for sure. Yes, maybe not. But they still, they're still very much in my brain because that was so shocking. I was like, oh, my God, I'm just so bad compared to everyone else. Now, I still have a vivid memory of those tests. That was just my worst nightmare going through those testing. It was terrible. Now, you spent you spent so much time with your father as a coach by your side throughout your tennis career. Was there a mechanism you were able to use to switch between coach and player to dad and daughter during your sort of childhood years? Yeah, that's a very interesting question. And it's definitely not easy to do. I mean, obviously, you guys had example in Australia when where it didn't work with Yelena Dochic, which is so sad when you read her story and everything she had to go through, it's horrible and it just breaks my heart. But obviously, for my dad being a doctor and having, you know, the psychological knowledge of how a young girl can function, how a young adult can function, how someone will respond in term of, you know, dealing with the stress basically daily, because as a tennis player, you're constantly under stress. It's not a match to play. It's some points to defend the title to defend. It's everything. Sometimes you have to defend, you know, 2000 points, let's say before the week starts when you have to defend a grand slam. So all of that pressure, it's really difficult, a human being.

So the way my dad was behaving with me was basically to give me my space outside of the tennis court. So I was always someone who really liked to constantly watch tennis matches. So I just had constantly tennis matches on the background. And then I always been quite autistic. So I was bringing my paints with me. I was doing painting when I was on the tour. I was doing Sudoku. I was constantly having my brain working, but constantly watching some tennis as well, which was not something my dad was doing at all. When he was, then we were finished with my tennis. He was not watching that much tennis. He was more into chess. So we had our own space outside of the tennis court, which was very delimited. So that's why actually a lot of parents and because of the lack of funding, basically at the beginning, they start to share the rooms where there are athletes, where there are kids. And this is where sometimes a problem can start because you're constantly with your child, you don't need them enough space to grow by themselves. And even though we were not having a lot of funding at the beginning, we might take cheaper hotels, but my dad was making sure I had my own space. And that comes down as well to being responsible. You know, so when I was having a match at nine a.m. in the morning, I had to put my own wake up alarm. I have to wake up myself and to go to a break of myself. And we were meeting, let's say, by the car to go to a tennis club,

but it was not the one waking home and waking me up in the morning and tell me I had a tennis match to play and all of that. So he gave me that responsibility and he gave me my space as well, which is, I think, very much crucial because you need to develop as a person and you need to find what what fits you outside of the tennis court as well. And you can't be 24 seven with the same person. You need to have your own, you know, space, I believe. I mean, that works for me. And I think if I look at other successful parents, daughter relationship, I can think of Caroline Wozniaki. I can think of Elena DeMantieva. I can think of Silvan Rafael Adar, which is very much a lot followed by his uncle and his dad as well. You know, they are their own space and the parents are present just for the support. Obviously, they're not tennis coaches. And if they're tennis coaches as well on top of it, then the present on the tennis part. But I strongly believe and I'm a strong advocate of separate the two things and give them enough space to grow as a person and, you know, believe in them in their face in that phase is when they will have responsibility and they will have to face them. And don't think because you're going to leave your child alone in the room. He's going to go out and party until 1 a.m. And then be fatigued for the next day. You know, you have to trust your child as well to take the right

to take the right steps forward, to do the right things and to be responsible for what he's doing. And in case he's doing a mistake, he will realize it by himself and he will not do it again. But if you try to force the issue by being sort of constantly around him and or her and to try to avoid a little small mistake they can do at the child is actually going to not turn up really well because you have a sort of rebellion that comes at some points and that rebellion is very dangerous, you know, moving down the road. So my father was very much giving me responsibility, was very much hard on the practice test for sure. I mean, that was well known. It was very strict. But when he was over, it was over. We were switching off, we were talking about something else. And it was the constant 24 hours, seven, you have to think about this. You have to think about that. You have to do this tomorrow. You have to do that. It was just when it was time for tennis, it was time for tennis. But when it was off and it was over, then it was really over. And when I look at King Richard film, you can very much see that as well. I mean, Richard and Oracita was present, but they still gave Serena some space to do something else, to do some dancing, to do some singing, to do something else outside of the tennis court. And I believe this is the right way to do it. Yes, some fantastic advice and insights into your your childhood there.

So thanks for sharing those as well. One of the questions that we're asking all of the presenters during this conference is you've got some coaches that are just starting off their coaching career that are listening in. What's three tips that you would give to a young coach just starting their career? So the three tips that we'll give is the first one. Always look for the child who is ready to do more. So don't look for the most talented one. And that's exactly what I said to Alicia the other day when we had that conference. Don't look for the most talented one. The one that has a look to have an easy strike. Look for the one that has that that's determination in the way they look at you and look for the ones who are going to be early in the practice and is going to leave later that what they're supposed to do. Look for that child because he has the most important thing, which is the determination and the will. You can always build a technique. You can always build a fitness, but to build a wheel, it's a lot more difficult. So look for that child and as your own way to train, especially with which I believe I'm a strong believer of the right technique. So especially in the fundamentals in the technique, obviously we all have different ways to hit the ball. But at the end of the day, the three or four fundamental points to hit the ball. Well, all of the protein is payers are doing it.

So make sure you have your facts right so you can really teach straight away the beginning when you have some youngsters coming at you the right technique. So they don't pick up some bad habits, which would be difficult to change down the road. So when I see sometimes some kids coming out of, you know, club training or whatever, and they're 10, 11 or 12, and the parents come to see me, I see horrible technique issues. And they have been doing it already, usually for four or five years. So yes, it's still time to change it, but it's starting to be a little bit dodgy and difficult. So really try to write at the beginning, even if they try to compensate by finding power elsewhere, give them the right technique habits. It will help them down the road. That would be my second tip and third tips. Never forget that any smart start with a serve and a return. And most of the time I see so often the serve being the last five percent of of a practice is really the last five minutes. And you just give them the basket and as them to do 20 serve and the practice is over and same for the return. And everything is just going from the back of the court or the body. But everything started with a serve and a return. So build that around your practice. Give enough time to those two shots. They're the most crucial shot in tennis. They're the one that was starting the points. And and then, of course, build the rest.

But don't, you know, consider those as a sort of the smallest ones at the end of practice, because ultimately as a player, you need a great serve, you need a good return. So that that is really for me, the three fundamental pillars, especially in the build up of a player that you have to be careful of. Well, thank you, Mary, and we could talk for hours and hours. But unfortunately, our time is is up this afternoon. But coaches, if you wanted to have the chance to win a one on one chat with Marion, please fill out the survey monkey at the conclusion of this conference, Marion, we thank you so much for your time. I've enjoyed every second of it. And and good luck with your play during the Australian Open. Thank you so much. It was my pleasure. Thank you.
